titleStmt.title: Exact schedulability analysis of systems based on single-rate periodic cyclic executives

analytic.title: Exact schedulability analysis of systems based on single-rate periodic cyclic executives

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In a recent survey of industry practitioners in the field of real-time systems, the majority of the respondents indicated that cyclic executives are in use in their systems. Unfortunately, contemporary text books hardly address cyclic executives, if at all. There is therefore a need for analysis techniques for these executives.

In this paper, we consider the single-rate periodic cyclic executive, scheduling a given sequence of independent hard real-time polling tasks in a single-processor system. We present exact analysis for this cyclic executive, and discuss its relative strengths and weaknesses compared to single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead. Unlike existing approaches, which typically take periodic tasks as a starting point for cyclic executives and focus on schedulability of tasks, we take the schedulability of the system as a starting point, i.e. whether or not the system meets its deadlines. In particular, we do not assume periods and deadlines for tasks, and our analysis derives feasible cycle times of a single-rate periodic cyclic executive for a system.

div.head: A. Background and motivation
div.p: In a recent survey of 120 industry practitioners in the field of real-time embedded systems [1], it was observed that from the 97 respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in the considered systems, 54.17% answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered". The academic interest in cyclic executives has gradually decreased over the last two decades, however, since it was concluded by C. Douglass Locke [2] that the fixed-priority approach generally dominates the cyclic executive approach for hard real-time systems. As a result, cyclic executives are mentioned in contemporary text books, such as [3]- [6], but hardly addressed in detail. Because cyclic executives are still in use in practice, proper explanation of cyclic executives and their exact analysis remains desirable, however. In earlier work, we therefore presented exact analysis for (basic) single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives [7]. This paper presents exact analysis for single-rate periodic cyclic executives, and discusses its relative strengths and weaknesses compared to single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead.

div.head: B. Problem description
div.p: Hard real-time systems require timely responses to events. As illustrated by an air bag, a system response (the inflation of an airbag) shall be provided in a well-defined interval relative to the occurrence of an event (a collision), i.e. neither too early nor too late. A system specification may therefore constrain the time-interval from an event to a response by both a lower bound, a so-called best-case system deadline, as well as an upper bound, a so-called worst-case system deadline. For hard real-time computing systems, where control is realized in software, these system deadlines give rise to timing constraints on the real-time tasks that have to detect events (through regularly polling sensors) and provide responses (using actuators).

In this paper, we assume a hard real-time system with a set of n (input) events, a set of n (output) responses, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Events are sporadic, i.e. are characterized by a minimal inter-arrival time. Each event-response tuple is characterized by a best-case system deadline and a worst-case system deadline, where the worst-case system deadline is at most equal to the minimal inter-arrival time of the event. Each event-response tuple is handled by a dedicated real-time polling task. A task detects an event through observation, e.g. by reading sensory data, and provides a response through a command, e.g. using an actuator; see Figure 1. We assume a single-processor system and a basic singlerate cyclic executive to schedule the set of tasks. In particular, we assume a statically known sequence of tasks executed in a continuous loop, in which every task occurs exactly once.
div.formula: System S τ 1 τ 2 τ n ...
div.p: Although tasks scheduled by means of a cyclic executive are typically assumed to be periodic [8], i.e. are typically assumed to be activated with a fixed inter-arrival time (or period), we do not make that 'software design step' in this paper. The problem addressed in this paper is (i) how to determine the schedulability of the system, i.e. whether or not the best-case and worst-case deadlines of the system are met, and (ii) which single-rate cyclic executive to choose.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, we present exact analysis for single-rate periodic cyclic executives. In addition, we discuss the relative strengths and weaknesses of the single-rate periodic cyclic executive compared with the single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead.

div.head: D. Organization
div.p: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we present a basic real-time system model. Section III provides a recap of the three basic single-rate cyclic executives considered. Exact worst-case analysis of the singlerate periodic cyclic executive is the topic of Section IV. A discussion on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the cyclic executives can be found in Section V. In Section VI, we briefly discuss a refinement of the periodic cyclic executive. We conclude the paper in Section VII.

div.head: II. A BASIC REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume a system S, a set E S of n sporadic (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Each event e i is characterized by a minimal interarrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple < e i , r i > is characterized by a best-case system deadline BD S i and a worstcase system deadline WD S i , where 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . Moreover, we assume a set T S of n independent polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , where task τ i senses event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i is characterized by a best-case computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , where 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The execution of a task is termed a job. A job of task τ i is denoted by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k, i.e. the first job of τ i is denoted by ι i,0 . The computation time C i,k of every job ι i,k of task τ i shall be between BC i and WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: We use s i,k and f i,k to denote the start time and the finalization time of job ι i,k , respectively. The start jitter SJ i of a task τ i is defined as the maximum deviation of the start-times of that task from a strictly periodic pattern, i.e.
div.formula: SJ i = sup 0≤k ∧ 0≤ ((s i,k -k × T i ) -(s i, -× T i )) , (1
div.p: where T i denotes the (assumed) period of the task. The finalization jitter is defined similarly, i.e.
div.formula: FJ i = sup 0≤k ∧ 0≤ ((f i,k -k × T i ) -(f i, -× T i )) . (2
div.p: We assume that tasks are scheduled by cyclic executives, run non-preemptively and do not suspend themselves. The sequence of tasks executed in a cycle is assumed to be known statically. Moreover, we ignore scheduling overhead and system initialization. When a system S meets all its deadlines under a specific cyclic executive and a specific sequence of tasks, the system S is called schedulable under that cyclic executive and that sequence.
For ease of presentation and without loss of generality, the jobs of tasks in a cycle are assumed to be executed in the order of increasing index, i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i<j≤n ∧ 0≤k s i,k < s j,k .
div.p: (3) III. A RECAP OF BASIC SINGLE-RATE CYCLIC EXECUTIVES For (basic) cyclic executives, tasks can simply be implemented as procedures and executed within a loop. A singlerate cyclic executive essentially executes every task exactly once in a cycle. In the following subsections, three basic types of single-rate cyclic executives are recapitulated, AFAP, timedriven AFAP, and periodic.

div.head: A. Single-rate AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: Figure 2 illustrates a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive. Note that the processor is constantly busy executing tasks.

div.head: B. Single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: For a single-rate time-driven AFAP, a cycle is started by a timer. The sum of the worst-case computation times of all tasks shall be less than the inter-arrival time T S of the timer, otherwise the (worst-case) executions of the tasks do not 'fit' in a cycle, i.e.
div.formula: 1≤i≤n WC i ≤ T S . (4
div.p: Figure 3 illustrates a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive with cycle time T S , where the cycle is started at time Φ. By starting cycles with an inter-arrival time of T S , the spare time, i.e. the combination of slack time 1 and gain time2 , can be used to execute background tasks or run the processor at a lower, more energy efficient, clock frequency after the cycle is completed.

div.head: C. Single-rate periodic cyclic executive
div.p: For a single-rate periodic cyclic executive, we focus on the 'strict' case, where every task is started at a specific time. In particular, for the 'strict' case we assume that every task is started at the worst-case start-time relative to the start of the cycle assuming each task needs its worst-case execution time. Similar to the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, the tasks shall 'fit' in a cycle, i.e. (4) must hold. Figure 4 illustrates such a single-rate periodic cyclic executive with cycle time T S .

In a 'non-strict' case, not all tasks are necessarily started at a statically determined time, but some may be started immediately after the previous task completed. Hence, the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive is a special case of a non-strict single-rate periodic cyclic executive.

div.head: IV. EXACT ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we first recapitulate an exact condition for the schedulability of a system S when tasks are scheduled by a basic cyclic executive. We subsequently present example systems, which we will use in the remainder of the section for illustration purposes. Next, we recapitulate the exact analysis for the single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven cyclic executive and present the exact analysis for the single-rate periodic cyclic executive. We conclude the section with remarks.

div.head: A. A recap of an exact schedulability condition
div.p: As described in [7], a system S meets its deadlines under a basic cyclic executive when the following schedulability condition holds
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∀ 0≤k f i,k+1 -s i,k ≤ WD S i ∧ BC i ≥ BD S i . (5)
div.p: The logical conjunction constituting this condition consists of two parts, a first part describing a worst-case schedulability condition, i.e. whether or not the system meets its worstcase deadlines, and a second part describing a best-case schedulability condition, i.e. whether or not a system meets its best-case deadlines.

The best-case schedulability condition is independent of a specific cyclic executive and checking the condition is considered trivial. We therefore focus on checking the worstcase schedulability condition.

Given the cyclic nature of the single-rate cyclic executive and the fact that every task is executed exactly once in the cycle, it is sufficient to consider at most 2, or 1 pair of, successive jobs of τ i . Hence, we can simplify the worst-case schedulability condition in (5) to
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n f i,1 -s i,0 ≤ WD S i . (6
div.p: To determine schedulability, we therefore have to test at most n conditions.

A COMPARISON OF BASIC CYCLIC EXECUTIVES In this section, we discuss the relative strengths and weaknesses of the single-rate periodic cyclic executive compared to the single-rate AFAP and the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives based on four dimensions, jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead.

div.head: A. Jitter
div.p: In this subsection, we consider start jitter as well as finalization jitter of tasks. We merely observe that start and finalization jitter may have an influence on control performance; see, for example, [10], [11].

1) Single-rate AFAP cyclic executive: As described in [7], a task τ i may experience unbounded start jitter or drift 4 under a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive when 1≤j≤n BC j < 1≤j≤n WC j . Given the fact that the start jitter is unbounded, it is immediately clear that the a task τ i may also experience unbounded finalization jitter.
2) Single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive: As described in [7], a task τ i may experience (bounded) start jitter SJ i under a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, which is given by
div.formula: SJ i = 1≤j<i (WC j -BC j ) .
div.p: The finalization jitter FJ i of a task τ i is simply found by adding execution jitter WC i -BC i to the start jitter SJ i , i.e.
div.formula: FJ i = 1≤j≤i (WC j -BC j ) .
div.p: 3) Single-rate periodic cyclic executive: Under a singlerate periodic cyclic executive, the start time s i,k of job ι i,k is exactly defined by
div.formula: s i,k = s 1,0 + k × T S + 1≤j<i WC j . (10
div.p: Stated differently, every task is started strictly periodically, i.e. ∀ 1≤i≤n SJ i = 0, making scheduling highly deterministic.
A task τ i may experience limited finalization jitter FJ i due to its execution jitter WC i -BC i , however, i.e.
div.formula: FJ i = WC i -BC i .

div.head: C. Schedulability
div.p: We first prove, using an auxiliary lemma, that the singlerate periodic cyclic executive can schedule more systems than the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, i.e. that the former dominates the latter from a scheduling perspective. We subsequently show that the single-rate periodic cyclic executive and the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive can schedule the same systems, i.e. are equivalent from a scheduling perspective.
Lemma 3. When a system S is schedulable under a singlerate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, it is also schedulable under a single-rate periodic cyclic executive.

Proof. We first recall from Section IV that the best-case schedulability condition is independent of the cyclic executive. To prove the lemma, we therefore only have to show that when the worst-case deadlines of S are met for a given sequence of tasks under a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, these deadlines are also met under a single-rate periodic cyclic executive. This result follows immediately by observing that (9) in Theorem 3 implies (8) in Theorem 2, because ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i ≤ WC i .
Theorem 4. From a scheduling perspective, the single-rate periodic cyclic executive dominates the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive.

Proof. Follows immediately from Lemma 3 and the fact that the single-rate periodic cyclic executive can schedule system S II , whereas the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive can not, irrespective of the order of the tasks in the sequence.

div.head: D. Implementation overhead
div.p: The single-rate AFAP cyclic executive has the lowest overhead of the three types of cyclic executives considered, i.e. only the execution of the while-loop contributes to the overhead. Unfortunately, the low overhead can not be exploited for other purposes.

The single-rate periodic cyclic executive has the highest overhead, due to the additional for-loop, the additional n -1 calculations of the value of time and the executions of the sleepuntil function; see Figure 4. Moreover, whenever the gain-time is used to run tasks in the background, that gaintime becomes available in a fragmented fashion, giving rise to additional context switches. As a result, for systems that (i) are schedulable by both the time-driven AFAP as well as the periodic cyclic executive, (ii) have similar values for the cycle time T S (just like system S I ) 5 and (iii) are not sensitive to start jitter or finalization jitter, a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive may therefore be preferred above a single-rate periodic cyclic executive.

div.head: E. Summary
div.p: Table IV briefly summarizes the comparison of the three basic single-rate cyclic executives in this section. Based on this comparison, we draw the following conclusion:
1) periodic preferred above AFAP: Apart from having a higher overhead, the single-rate periodic cyclic executive outperforms the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive.

div.head: 2) periodic typically preferred above a time-driven AFAP:
div.p: Given the dominance of the single-rate periodic cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective, it is typically preferred above the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. We used typically in our second conclusion, because the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive may be preferred above the single-rate periodic cyclic executive for specific cases; see Section V-D.

div.head: VI. DISCUSSION
div.p: In this paper, we focussed on the 'strict' case of singlerate periodic cyclic executives, where every task is started at a specific time; see Section III-C. The 'non-strict' case, where not all tasks are necessarily started at a statically determined time, but some may be started immediately after the previous task completed, may provide options to reduce both the implementation overhead and the fragmentation of spare time compared to the 'strict' case. As already mentioned in Section III-C, the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive can be viewed as a special case of a 'non-strict' single-rate periodic cyclic executive.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we considered scheduling of independent, 'regularly' polling tasks on a single processor using a ('strict') single-rate periodic cyclic executive. Unlike existing approaches, that take a 'software design step' by assuming periods and deadlines for tasks, we focussed on whether or not the deadlines of the system are met. A major advantage of our approach is that there is no need to decide upon the specific periods and deadlines of the tasks to determine schedulability of the system.

We presented exact analysis for single-rate periodic cyclic executives. Because best-case analysis turned out to be trivial, focus of this paper has been on exact worst-case analysis (Theorem 3). Our analysis derives feasible cycle times of a single-rate periodic cyclic executive for a system. Next, we discussed the relative strengths and weaknesses of the singlerate periodic cyclic executive compared to the single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead. In particular, we provided two schedulability related proofs. Firstly, we proved that the single-rate periodic cyclic executive dominates the single-rate time-driven AFAP from a scheduling perspective (Theorem 4). Secondly, we proved that the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive and the single-rate periodic cyclic executive are equivalent from a scheduling perspective (Theorem 5). Although the single-rate periodic cyclic executives will typically be the preferred type of single-rate cyclic executive, we identified specific cases where a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive may be preferred.

Investigating the 'non-strict' case of a single-rate periodic cyclic executive, is a topic of future work. The impact of refinements and extensions of the basic real-time system model, such as taking the notion of observable event [13] or the single-path code paradigm [14] into account, on the schedulability analysis of single-rate cyclic executives is another topic of future work.
